title: Private Deployments Reference Guide
author: Ava Chen
content:
Overview

This document is the canonical reference for Redwood Inference private deployments. It consolidates deployment guides for VPC-based installs, reference architectures for cloud and on-prem environments, the on-prem packaging and installer options, Day-2 operational guidance, upgrade and rollback procedures, and a customer requirements library used during pre-sales and onboarding.

Scope

- Target audience: SREs, platform engineers, customer engineering (solutions), and enterprise customers implementing private deployments (VPC and on-prem).
- Environments covered: cloud VPC (AWS, GCP, Azure), private VPC with cross-account peering, and air-gapped on-prem installations (VM and Kubernetes).
- Not covered: hosted Redwood API onboarding (see product docs) and local development quickstarts.

Quick links

- Reference architecture diagrams: see the "Reference architectures" section below for ASCII/diagram descriptions.
- Installer artifacts: helm charts, VM images, and tarball checksums are published to the private artifact bucket (customer-specific access required).
- Support runbooks: see Day-2 operations section and the eng-oncall runbooks.

1) Roles and ownership

- Owner: eng-private-deployments team (primary contact: customer-eng@redwood.ai).
- Deployment owner (customer): assigned on contract signature. Redwood provides an onboarding engineer for Dedicated/Private enterprise packages.
- SRE: responsible for global SLO monitoring and cross-region fallbacks for multi-region VPC designs.

2) Prerequisites and customer requirements (summary table)

| Requirement area | Minimum expectation | Notes / example values |
|---|---:|---|
| Network connectivity | Routed subnets with NAT/Bastion | 2 private subnets per AZ, 1 public for NAT/bastion |
| IP addressing | CIDR block with 100+/usable IPs per AZ | Avoid overlapping with customer VPN ranges |
| Cloud accounts | Dedicated service account / IAM role with least privilege | See IAM policy template in appendix |
| GPUs & compute | At least one GPU node pool (A100/V100/RTX6000 class) | Node size depends on model footprint and q8/q4 quantization profiles |
| Storage | 1–5 TiB encrypted block storage + S3-compatible object store | Use lifecycle policy for model cache tiers |
| KMS / keys | Customer-managed KMS key | Required for M+ security package (bring-your-own-key) |
| Audit logging | Centralized audit/logging sinks (CloudWatch/Stackdriver/ELK) | 90-day retention minimum for audit; 365d for forensic packages |
| Network egress | Configured NAT or private link for repo/artifact access | See offline install section for air-gapped flows |

3) Reference architectures (high-level descriptions)

A. VPC (single-account, multi-AZ) - Recommended for most enterprise customers
- Components: private subnets for inference nodes, public subnets for bastion/NAT, management subnet for control-plane components (console, metrics forwarder), dedicated GPU node pools, object storage (S3) for model artifacts, and central logging.
- Diagram (textual):
  - VPC CIDR: 10.0.0.0/16
  - Subnets: 10.0.1.0/24 (public), 10.0.2.0/24 (private-az1), 10.0.3.0/24 (private-az2)
  - Peering: Optional VPC peering to customer app VPC; route table entries for 10.1.0.0/16 app CIDR.

B. Multi-account / hub-and-spoke (recommended for large orgs)
- Components: central networking account (transit gateway), per-team workloads in spoke accounts, centralized logging and artifact repositories, cross-account IAM roles for deployment automation.

C. On-prem (air-gapped, Kubernetes)
- Components: on-prem K8s cluster (1+ master, N worker nodes with GPUs), private artifact registry (Harbor), internal object store (minio), local KMS or HSM stub for secrets, and an optional jumpbox for operator access.
- Diagram (textual):
  - Management plane (operator workstation) -> bastion -> kube-api -> inference pods (GPU nodes)
  - Artifact flows are pulled from a pre-seeded registry (no direct internet).

4) VPC Deployment guide (step-by-step)

This section describes the common VPC install pattern using our helm-based installer and Terraform for infra bootstrapping. Steps assume AWS but map 1:1 to other clouds:

Prereqs: Terraform v1.5+, kubectl v1.26+, helm v3.12+, AWS CLI v2 with deploy role access. Customer must provide a service IAM role with the policies in the appendix.

Step 1 - Prepare network
1. Allocate CIDR and create VPC with at least two private subnets across AZs.
2. Create public subnets for NAT/bastion and attach an Internet Gateway.
3. Create route tables: private subnets route to NAT gateway; public routes to IGW.
4. (Optional) Configure VPC peering or Transit Gateway with application VPCs.

Step 2 - Provision compute and storage
1. Use Terraform module redwood-gpu-nodepool to provision a node pool with GPU instances. Example: g4dn.12xlarge or A100 variants.
2. Attach encrypted EBS volumes with throughput tuned to model loading (recommend io2 for higher IOPS).
3. Create S3 buckets with encryption and lifecycle rules. Grant the Redwood service role access.

Step 3 - Deploy control plane and runtime
1. Install cert-manager and the cluster ingress controller.
2. Inject KMS secret provider (external-secrets or cloud-provider KMS plugin).
3. Helm install redwood-runtime-chart --namespace redwood --set ingress.domain=private.example.com --set modelCache.sizeGb=500 --set kvCache.enabled=true
4. Validate pods: kubectl -n redwood get pods and ensure all containers are READY.

Step 4 - Network hardening and security
1. Lock down security groups: only allow ports 443 (control plane), 10250 (kubelet) from bastion and management CIDRs.
2. Configure egress rules: allow only required artifact registries and telemetry endpoints.
3. Enable VPC Flow Logs and forward to centralized logging.

Step 5 - Smoke tests and onboarding
1. Run the smoke script: scripts/smoke/run_smoke.sh (will generate a small inference request, validate latency, and check model loading).
2. Run the eval suite for one pinned model and verify output stability.
3. Onboard first model via the operator UI or CLI and confirm model pulls and cache population.

5) On-prem packaging and install options

We provide three packaging forms depending on customer needs: Helm chart (recommended for K8s), VM images (OVA/AMI-like for hypervisor-based installs), and an air-gapped tarball with pre-seeded artifact registry metadata.

- Helm chart notes:
  - Charts are parameterized; typical toggles: resourceClass (gpu/cpu), quantizationProfile (q8f16/q4), modelCache.sizeGb, and nodeSelector labels.
  - Post-install hook will run the initial model-lifecycle job to seed the model cache.

- VM images / appliance:
  - OVA bundles include: runtime binary, model cache layout, local docker registry, and a minimal management UI. Requires customer virtualization infra (ESXi/Hyper-V).
  - Image sizes range 40–120GB depending on included model cache.

- Air-gapped tarball:
  - Contains: helm chart, container images (tar.gz), model artifact bundles, and installation checklist.
  - Install flow: seed registry -> apply helm charts with --set offline=true -> run registry-sync job.

Packaging checklist (table):

| Package type | Required customer artifacts | Operator actions |
|---|---|---|
| Helm (online) | kube creds, service account, KMS key | helm install + post-install model seed |
| Helm (air-gapped) | local registry, pre-seeded images, install checklist | load images -> helm install --set offline=true |
| Appliance (OVA) | ESXi or Hyper-V access, IP allocation | import OVA -> configure network -> run setup script |

6) Day-2 operations (runbook highlights)

Monitoring & alerting
- Core metrics to monitor: per-node GPU utilization, model-load latency (target < 300ms for small models, < 800ms for large 8K-context models), per-route P95 and P99 token latencies, cache hit ratio (target > 80% for steady state), and queue depth.
- SLOs (example):
  - Availability: 99.95% for control-plane APIs (monthly).
  - Inference latency: P95 < 350ms for short-context models under normal load.
  - Error rate: <0.5% for 5xx on inference endpoints.

Logging and traces
- Forward application logs and traces to the centralized telemetry stack (OTel-compatible). Use the provided log-parser to map model IDs, request IDs, and cost metrics. Retention defaults: 90d for metrics, 180d for traces (configurable).

Capacity planning and autoscaling
- Use historical token-per-second metrics to plan GPU node counts. A rule of thumb: 1 A100-80GB can serve ~150-400 tokens/s for GPT-sized models depending on quantization.
- Configure HPA/Cluster-Autoscaler with node-provisioning cooldowns (10m) to avoid thrash. Burst pools: maintain a small warm pool of on-demand instances for 10% burst traffic.

Operational playbooks (summary)
1. Model stuck in provisioning: check image pull errors, registry credentials, and disk pressure. Restart model lifecycle job if necessary.
2. High latency incidents: verify cache hit ratio, GPU saturation, and network egress throttling. Temporarily route traffic to fallback smaller model if overloaded.
3. Node failure: cordon and drain, replace node via Terraform or cloud autoscaling; validate model cache warming on replacement nodes.

7) Upgrade and rollback procedures

Upgrade principles
- Prefer rolling upgrades with canary traffic for control plane and runtime. Use semantic versioned helm charts and keep a documented compatibility matrix for model artifact formats.
- Backups: always take a full snapshot of the metadata DB, model registry index, and the KMS key policy before any upgrade.

Canary/rolling upgrade steps (example)
1. Create a canary control-plane deployment: helm upgrade --set canary.enabled=true --set replicaCount=1.
2. Route 5–10% of traffic to canary via traffic-split (service mesh or ingress split).
3. Monitor key metrics for 30–60 minutes: error rate, P95 latency, and memory pressure.
4. If stable, progressively increase to 25%, 50%, then 100% with validation windows.

Rollback steps (fast failure)
1. Immediately revert ingress traffic to previous revision (traffic-split rollback).
2. helm rollback <release> <revision> for control-plane or runtime charts.
3. If DB migrations were applied that are not reversible, restore from snapshot and replay any committed changes as needed.
4. Post-rollback: run smoke tests and run a reduced eval suite to ensure functional parity.

Database and state considerations
- Migrations: follow the practice of backward-compatible DB migrations (expand-then-contract). Coordinate migration windows with the customer for larger schema changes.
- Model cache: model artifact formats must be compatible; if not, include a migration step that re-seeds models into the new cache layout in parallel.

8) Customer requirements library (detailed checklist)

Use this library during presales and onboarding to capture requirements and map to deployment patterns. Copy this checklist into the onboarding ticket.

- Networking
  - Preferred cloud and region(s)
  - CIDR allocations for VPC and application VPCs
  - Allowed egress destinations (artifact registries, telemetry endpoints)
  - Transit/peering requirements and VPN details

- Security & compliance
  - Required certifications (SOC2, ISO27001, HIPAA) and evidence needs
  - KMS/HSM requirements and key rotation policy
  - Audit log retention period and export formats
  - Data residency constraints and any special masking needs

- Compute & storage
  - Target model families and peak QPS expectations
  - GPU types and minimum memory per GPU
  - Persistent storage size and IOPS requirements

- Observability & operations
  - Central telemetry endpoints (OTel collector host/port)
  - Pager schedule and escalation contacts
  - On-call rotation for customer-managed ops vs Redwood-managed support tiers

- Business/contractual
  - SLA targets and penalty clauses
  - Maintenance windows and lead times for major upgrades
  - Support tier and included run-hours for onboarding assistance

9) Appendix: templates and example commands

IAM policy snippet (example placeholder):
- s3:GetObject, s3:ListBucket for model buckets
- kms:Decrypt for model key access
- ec2:Describe* for node discovery

Terraform snippet (network module usage):
- module "redwood_vpc" { source = "git::ssh://git@repo/internal/terraform-modules.git//vpc" cidr = "10.0.0.0/16" }

Helm install example:
- helm repo add redwood https://artifacts.redwood.internal/charts
- helm install redwood-runtime redwood/runtime --namespace redwood --create-namespace --set ingress.domain=private.example.com

Smoke test summary (what it checks):
1. Control plane endpoints respond 200
2. Model fetch and load completes within configured timeout (default 120s)
3. Inference response returns valid JSON and latency within expected bounds
